en: The news from the Lotus Land concerns the true substance of the mind-body: pure, clear, and luminous; it does not belong to any one side, yet it fully encompasses all phenomena.
However, through a single thought from time immemorial, ignorance suddenly arose, whereby within this fundamentally pure state, empty space and the great earth manifested—just as, for example:
Within the lamp there is a mirror; within the mirror there is a lamp. The six realms and four modes of birth are layered upon one another without end.
All sages and all ordinary beings alike emerge from the world, reflecting and manifesting in a continuous cycle, ceaselessly transforming and delivering others. How far-reaching is this!

From the time of human birth—ten months of bloody impurity and three years of turbid milk—from one lifetime through many lifetimes, sentient beings take the shadow of conditions as their mind and the four great elements as their body.
The body undergoes birth and death; form and spirit circulate in flux. One cannot mend the leaks at the heart of the river, yet in vain one increases the sorrows within a dream.

There are a thousand varieties of suffering and joy, and ten thousand transformations of kindness and enmity. Though cause and effect are perfectly clear, those caught in the midst of it remain utterly deluded—this is truly a matter for deep lamentation.
This book explains these matters layer by layer, stripping away the coarse and common to reveal a subtle, profound essence that gives rise to all wonders and returns [to the source].
The *Jia yilu* (A Record of the Family Lineage) guides me forward. The text of the Nine Grades reveals the extraordinary skillful means for rebirth in the Pure Land.
May all virtuous women, together with the assembly of donors, carve this into woodblocks and circulate it.

By dedicating this merit, may all sentient beings be benefited, be born together in peace and happiness, and witness the perfect manifestation of the Pure Land. May the Sahā world suddenly become empty; may the Buddha-land be our home, and may the lotus flowers bloom.
Sufficient. Like the reflection in a mirror of radiant light, there is not the slightest trace of flaw; do not allow further transmigration to give rise to various [phenomena].
Written in the winter of the tenth year of the Tongzhi era by Miaokongzi at his dwelling amidst the misty waters of a hundred cities.
*Lianbang xiaoxi* (News from the Lotus Land), Table of Contents.
Chapter One: The Radiance of Essential Nature and Phenomenal Marks; Chapter Two: Turning Away from Enlightenment to Unite with Dust;
Chapter Three: The Cycle of Samsara and Its Ceasing; Chapter Four: The Causes and Conditions for the Pure Land;
Chapter Five: Unflagging Diligence; Chapter Six: The Mutual Accordance of Samādhi and Prajñā.
Chapter Seven: The Manifestation in Every Thought-Moment; Chapter Eight: Entering the Stage of Rebirth;
Chapter Nine: The Perfect Interfusion of Body and Land (Appendix).
Ten Songs of Dwelling Clouds (On the Ten Evils) — Yan Yicheng Miaoxian’s *Línjiāngxiān* (Breaking the Ten Evils)
— Composed by the Chan Immortal Yuchi as a Message from the Lotus Land.
Chapter One: The Radiance of Essential Nature and Characteristics. O virtuous ones!
Having shared a karmic affinity from former lives, you have come together to hear the Dharma. As I am about to proclaim the sublime meaning, first purify your minds;

let your bodies and speech be composed and free from all agitation. You should offer the incense and flowers of faith and wisdom from within your hearts, extending your devotion with single-minded focus. Ten.
Now that the worthy and sages together unfold this sublime sound, do not treat it with indifference or deem it easy.
He manifests his power of mastery and speaks according to the subtle capacities of beings; Innumerable sentient beings all receive the prediction of rebirth in the Western Land.
Among the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, Amitābha is foremost.
Saving sentient beings through the nine grades, their majestic virtue is inexhaustible and the Buddha’s power is boundless.
Even now, everyone can recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha. How excellent! How excellent!
"Namo Amitābha Buddha"—these six characters, do you all understand them? *Namo* means "to take refuge in. *A* means "non-" or "without.
*Mita* means "measure" or "limit. *Buddha* means "luminous awakening. Thus, Amitābha Buddha is the immeasurable light within the hearts of every person.
O virtuous ones, you all arise from within this immeasurable light.
Come. You shall surely return to the midst of immeasurable radiance. Reflect for yourselves:
where do your current bodies and minds reside? Are they united with or separate from this immeasurable radiance? Are they one or two?

Fundamentally, it has neither beginning nor end; why need one distinguish between the provisional and the real? When you concentrate your spirit and contemplate, you shall see the person of original nature.
You should know that the luminosity of the original nature is originally without boundaries; it flows on without interruption. Amitābha appears before you precisely because of this.
There is no beginning. A single moment of non-awakening suddenly gives rise to ignorance, causing one to transmigrate through birth and death; therefore, one does not see it.
Thus, Śākyamuni Buddha, within this Sahā world, manifested the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, appearing from emptiness to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings.
The ocean of worlds is utterly empty; the wheel of space is vast and boundless. Within the dust-motes of all lands, the Tathāgatas manifest and guide beings according to their capacities.
In every land and within every mote of dust, purity and defilement are each distinguished; infinite causes and effects arise and fall in successive layers. This is the realm in which we dwell.
"In this Sahā world, our original teacher Śākyamuni is now about to enter parinirvāṇa; there is no Buddha to be seen here.
Beyond this Sahā world, proceeding westward for a hundred thousand *koṭis* of Buddha-lands, there is a realm called the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
There currently resides a Buddha named Amitābha, who is preaching the Dharma therein."
The two Honored Ones divide the two lands, saving the deluded multitudes through the Dharma; they urge those dwelling in the East to turn their minds and head directly toward the West.
As the Sūtra says: "The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction; for this reason, he is titled [Amitābha]."
Amitābha. Since he illuminates the lands of the ten directions, he will certainly not abandon this Sahā world.

Since he possesses immeasurable light, he must surely possess manifold spiritual responses. Therefore, by reciting his name even once, one immediately attains rebirth there and receives his transformative teaching.
Originally manifesting from within the mind, its light encompasses many worlds.

From this moment forth, proceeding directly, in every thought-moment one beholds Amitābha—the Buddha within the minds of sentient beings and the sentient beings within the mind of the Buddha. It is like two mirrors joined together; their radiance is no different.

Reflections appear within the light; ten thousand reflections are but a single light. Therefore, people of today—regardless of whether they are old or young, wise or foolish—when joy reaches its peak, they call upon Amitābha Buddha;
when suffering reaches its peak, they call upon Amitābha Buddha. This occurs whenever they encounter any matter or circumstance.
All are these four characters, for light is non-dual.

Those with the conditions shall all receive deliverance; long have they been imbued with the Buddha’s grace. To transform the multitudes of this Sahā world, the light emerges from the river of craving.
The radiance is non-dual, yet bodies and lands are manifold. If one wishes to emerge from the world, how could one not know the characteristics of the world?
When the world first arises, it first forms a wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) within the void, revolving with steady intensity;

this is what is evoked by the karmic consciousness of sentient beings. From within the wind, clouds arise; from within the clouds, rain falls, pouring down in vast torrents, which the wind-circle sustains.
Within the wind-circle, the Iron Encircling Mountains arise; all the great oceans are within these mountains. In the midst of the oceans, there are seven golden mountains.
Within the oceans on all four sides, the four great continents and their respective minor islands arise. Inside the seven golden mountains, [the central mountain stands].
Furthermore, fragrant water-oceans arise; within these fragrant water-oceans, Mount Sumeru arises.

On the mid-slopes of Mount Sumeru, there are four terraces on its four sides where the Four Heavenly Kings reside; this is called the first heaven. The sun and moon revolve around the mountain’s waist as they pass by.
The summit of the mountain is broad and level. On each of its four sides are eight celestial kings, with the Jade Emperor at the center, who governs all the heavens;
this is called the Heaven of the Thirty-three. In reality, it is the second heaven. These two heavens are those that dwell upon the earth.
The third is the Yāma Heaven, the fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven, the fifth is the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the sixth is the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; these are all situated within the clouds.

These dwellings collectively constitute the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). There is a class of beings who are not devas, called asuras; they possess the fortune of devas but lack their virtue.
From the heavens of the desire realm down to the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts, they dwell in intermixture with humans.
Animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings endure unspeakable suffering and are termed the three evil paths (*tridurgati*). Devas, humans, and asuras are termed the three good realms (*trisugati*).
The Path is divided into male and female. In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), beings sleep, compete for wealth and food, and kill one another; it is merely called the "Desire Realm.

Above this is the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), where there is only the physical body and all are exclusively male. They constantly abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and do not employ their bodies or speech.
Such is the Form Realm, which has four levels. Above the Form Realm is the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which likewise has four levels.
The characteristics of the Sahā world: It fundamentally rests upon a wind-wheel sphere.
Above it, the orbs of the sun and moon illuminate these mountains, seas, and continents. There dwell the gods of the Cloud-Abode and Earth-Abode heavens;
Ascending further to the First Dhyāna, one pushes out again and again— A thousand times a thousand, a thousand times a thousand; A thousand sets of a thousand times a thousand.
Named the Great Trichiliocosm, the Flower Adornment Ocean of Realms is profound; it reflects within the formless realm the diagram of small worlds.
This is the first of the Four Heavenly Kings’ Heavens.
The second is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, known as the Earth-Dwelling Devas; the third is the Yāma Heaven;
and the fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven. [The fifth is] the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
The fifth is Nirmāṇarati; the sixth is Paranirmita-vaśavartin, known as the Cloud-Dwelling Heaven.
These are the three tiers of heavens belonging to the first dhyāna. They are situated in...
Above the six heavens of the desire realm are:
the Brahmakāyika Heaven as the seventh,
the Brahmapurohita Heaven as the eighth, and the Mahābrahmā Heaven.
The ninth heaven. Extending upward from Mahābrahmā and downward to the Cakravāḍa mountains,
it is supported by a single wind-circle, named...
It constitutes a small world system.
In the diagram of a small thousand-world system,
each individual small world is reduced in scale.
This constitutes one point. In this manner,
there is one second-dhyāna heaven that governs a thousand such small world-systems.
This is called a small chiliocosm.
A small chiliocosm is one thousand [worlds].
The tenth is the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha). There is no...
The eleventh is the Heaven of Measured Light;
the twelfth is the Heaven of Luminous Sound.
These are collectively named the Heavens of the Second Dhyāna.
In this diagram of the intermediate chiliocosm,
each small chiliocosm is reduced to a single point. Thus...
One thousand small chiliocosms are governed by one single Heaven of the Third Dhyāna;
this is called a medium chiliocosm. Within [the medium chiliocosm]...
"Thousand" refers to two thousand.
The Heaven of Limited Purity is the thirteenth;
the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity is the tenth.
Fourth, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven;
these fifteen together are called the third dhyāna heaven.
In each diagram of the trichiliocosm,
every one of the intermediate chiliocosms is reduced to a single point; thus it is.
One thousand middle chiliocosms are governed by a single Cāturmahārājakāyika heaven;
this is called a great trichiliocosm. Great.
A thousand refers to the three-thousandfold world system.
A thousand times a thousand makes ten million; therefore, it is called "three thousand.
This is the first heaven of the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava).
Sixteen. Seventeenth, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven.
Eighteenth, the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
These are collectively termed the fourth [dhyāna].
The dhyāna heavens.
A map of world-systems as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field,
encompassing this trichiliocosm.
The worlds are shattered into minute particles;
each individual particle becomes a great trichiliocosm,
termed a "world-system as numerous as motes of dust."
Regarding the realms: within this, the number of worlds is extremely vast;
such is called a world as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field.
Adding two or three more,
they constitute two *kṣetraparamāṇurajaḥ* worlds or three *kṣetraparamāṇurajaḥ* worlds.
A single lotus-flower world-ocean is depicted within the infinite lotuses of the Flower Adornment Dharma-realm;
in each and every one of them—
All manifest immeasurable oceans of worlds.
That wherein we dwell is a single lotus at the very center of these. This...
The flower manifests twenty tiers of worlds.
The first tier consists of worlds as numerous as the atoms within a single *kṣetra*. The second tier...
In the twentieth layer above, within worlds as numerous as the atoms of two buddha-fields,
there are twenty worlds as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field.
Saha and Sukhāvatī are situated at the center of the thirteenth layer of worlds.
This small world-system in which we dwell was, at the time of its initial formation, the Ābhāsvara Heaven within the Second Dhyāna.

The devas descended from the void, each possessing the power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhi*) and moving with sovereign ease through the air. Because they consumed the "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*), their bodies became heavy and their radiance vanished;
they were no longer able to fly upward and thus became sentient beings upon the earth. After a long time, they divided into the two genders of male and female.
The fertility of the earth ceased to produce [spontaneously] and instead produced grains such as rice; though harvested in the morning, they grew back by evening, inexhaustible and endless.

When the greed of sentient beings arose, there came abundance and scarcity; once harvested, they no longer regrew, leading to further strife and plunder. Consequently, fields were divided, and each person cultivated their own portion.
He established the lords of the fields to govern the multitude; they were named Kṣatriyas, which refers to the class of kings. Through many successive reigns, there were both ordinary and holy kings.
Ordinary kings remained fixed upon the earth, while holy kings were able to travel through the air by means of their flying wheels. This lineage continued until the time of King Śuddhodana.
There were four brothers, each ruling over their own territory. The queen was named Lady Māyā.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was in the inner palace of the Tuṣita Heaven as the Bodhisattva of the Succession, known by the name Vimalaprabha (Hùmíng). He manifested as a white elephant.
He entered the mother’s mouth and was born after ten months.
He was named Prince Siddhārtha, the fourth of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Initially descending from the Tuṣita Heaven as a white elephant, he entered his mother’s mouth and was born emerging from her right side.
Pointing one finger to heaven and one finger to earth, he alone is the Most Honored One above and below the heavens.
A youth complete in both civil and martial arts, possessing the merit of a Wheel-Turning King yet refusing it, he conceived a child within the womb of his consort;
having thus ensured the succession for his father, he immediately left the home life.
Having realized through six years of ascetic practice that his path was entirely mistaken, he attained perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment.

He then extensively expounded the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, followed by the *Āgama* in the second period, the *Vaipulya* in the third and fourth, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and finally the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Having completed the work of delivering all sentient beings, he entered parinirvāṇa.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all great beings (mahāsattvas) shall uphold and practice the Buddha-dharma to deliver all sentient beings.
Among the three gates of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, each ultimately points back to the nature of the mind. The final expedient means is called the Pure Land Dharma Gate;

this is precisely to rely on the *Amitābha Sūtra* to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. As for the assembly at Maitreya’s Dragon Flower [Tree] in this world, it requires eight... [years/aeons].
Even if one were to live for over one million seven hundred thousand years, it would not equal the merit of being born early in the Western Land to hear Amitābha Buddha preach the Dharma in person.
Solemnly and earnestly praise Amitābha and the magnificently adorned realm of Sukhāvatī; may all people without exception swiftly depart for the West.
This Amitābha Buddha possesses immeasurable radiance and is thus also named Amitābha (Infinite Light) Buddha; his lifespan is immeasurable and he is thus also named Amitāyus (Infinite Life) Buddha.
His light being immeasurable signifies the vastness of those he delivers; his lifespan being immeasurable signifies the longevity of his work in delivering sentient beings.
Among the myriad phenomena of the world, names are distinguished and characteristics are established; when viewed with the physical eye, they appear to be manifold, yet through the wisdom-eye...
Upon observing it, one sees that it is nothing but immeasurable light. Thus, the ancients said: "The Amitābha of one's own nature is eternally pure;
the Pure Land of the sole mind has no boundaries."
Supremely wondrous and supremely subtle, it is straight without curvature; neither shallow nor deep, the Buddha’s capacity is inherently complete.
A person of great root and great vessel, upon merely being presented with this single phrase "Buddha," immediately penetrates it clearly, without any doubt.
When one is free from all obstructions and the Buddha-dharma is perfectly complete, then Amitābha is one’s own nature and the Pure Land is one’s own mind.
This is clearly manifest right now; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it is all one’s own original radiance. How could there be a journey of ten million billion lands?

It is simply a matter of the single mind remaining undistracted. If you have not yet attained awakening, birth and death will continue for a long time. Therefore, simply take up the single phrase "Amitābha."

Diligently maintain mindfulness until it reaches a state of single-mindedness without distraction. Suddenly, the flower of the mind blooms with clarity, and the realm of the Buddha is revealed as primordially present.
Only then does one realize that everything is entirely one's own nature, not something to be sought from another. Furthermore, there are those who do not understand the Dharma of awakening;
yet because their practice of nianfo (recitation of the Buddha’s name) is powerful, their habitual tendencies gradually diminish and lighten, like polishing a mirror.
The wheel turns; after a long time, one attains spontaneous illumination. With single-mindedness and without distraction, one beholds the Buddha and is reborn in the Pure Land.

This is the shortcut for spiritual cultivation, wondrously capable of encompassing and delivering those of all three faculties simultaneously. Within the Great Radiance, as days come and months pass, beings are transformed and delivered in an endless succession.
A single radiance shines throughout the ten directions; Majestic and immovable, the King of Dharma.
When the three calamities arise in boundless worlds, The Pure Land stands tall with its banner of seven treasures.
The light of Amitābha is originally boundless, Pervading the great earth, empty space, and the distant heavens.
Where is this place where beings find their refuge? Blue, yellow, red, white, and purple-gold lotuses bloom;

There are no more demons, heretics, or weapons of war. A single expanse of radiant glory reveals the Buddha, As all noble and virtuous ones gather together, With transformed birds and celestial music abounding throughout the six periods of the day.
How wondrous! A single thought evokes the Western Land; Through being received and led there, one attains great auspiciousness.
In this Sahā world, which is truly fraught with heat and affliction, It is better to return [to that land] and find immediate coolness.
From within the light, he spoke of this World of Ultimate Bliss; Whether wise or foolish, all shall surely be reborn there. It is as in the *Dhyāna-sūtra*:

The five schools of the Chan lineage (Linji, Caodong, Guiyang, Fayan, and Yunmen; today only the Linji and Caodong schools remain). The three schools of the Exegetical tradition (Tiantai, Xianshou, and Ci'en;
Tiantai established the Four Teachings, Xianshou established the Five Teachings, while Ci'en specialized exclusively in the Yogācāra school of the Dharma-character [Xiangzong]).

The one school of the Vinaya tradition, as well as all those who practice without specializing in a particular method, must each rely on their own capacity to recite the Buddha’s name for rebirth in the Pure Land, thereby entering the nine grades of rebirth. Only then...
One is able to be non-retrogressive. To be non-retrogressive means not retreating from Bodhi. Is this not the single mind of this radiance?
Completing my own measure of the single mind, reciting the name of Amitābha, the oceans of lands in the ten directions will from now on cease their frantic toil.

In the second chapter, "Turning Away from Enlightenment and Joining with Dust," within the Great Second Radiance, all is perfectly complete without the need for artificial arrangement. Since one is deluded regarding original enlightenment, this is itself ignorance.

Now, the essence of the true void is a radiance that eternally fills the ten directions. That sentient beings have transmigrated through the cycles of saṃsāra for kalpas is solely because they do not know that there is a Buddha.
Thus, boundless darkness arises; the void is born within awakening, and the jewel is lost within one's own clothing as soon as emotion is produced.
Wisdom has already been severed. If one does not eliminate delusions regarding the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, there will be no end to this state at all.
As the ancients said: "Entering the sea to count its sands is to know only how to weary oneself. They also said: "If one dwells long among humans and devas, evil karma will surely arise.

Alas! This is true even for those in the human realm; how much more so for those in the three miserable paths? To be devoid of spiritual efficacy life after life and to cut off the path to the sages is most lamentable. Life and death—
They arise in succession; water and fire contend with one another. Karmic retribution persists and returns; the links of the chain do not cease. Truly, one does not know where it will end.
From a single delusive thought, one commits killing, stealing, and lust. This is what constitutes evil.
(Delusive thoughts) obscurely enter the dream, and one takes them to be real. Thus, one treats the gatekeeper as the master.
They give rise to the affairs of boundless birth and death; Time and again they enter and exit, like guests and bandits meeting.
Contending and killing one another, when will it ever cease? They exchange skulls and yet harbor further enmity;
Whether intentional or unintentional, all is karmic retribution. They take the lives of others as their precious delicacies.
(Stealing) Day and night they are busily occupied, finding no leisure; when will their gold and jade ever accumulate like mountains?
The seats of gods and humans shift in turn, and the treasury-guarding wealth deities change their shifts as well.
(Lust) This body originally came from an error; yet one further draws in the vulgar womb through worldly charm.
One has personally gone to the hells of the iron bed and copper pillar; the various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been reduced to ashes.
That one was unaware while alive is already lamentable; how can one possibly master one’s own destiny in the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) after death? A hundred years are but a fleeting moment.
When the time of life’s end arrives, all the good and evil of one’s entire life will manifest simultaneously, along with all the karmic creditors from past lives and this present existence.
It is so. It is utterly impossible to evade; even the slightest transgression is reflected by the Mirror of Karma. One’s soul follows it and falls accordingly.

Even for those whose deeds are balanced between good and evil, or those who have not yet been subjected to investigation, there is drifting through seven births and seven deaths—this too is extreme suffering.
Once the retribution is fixed, there is no way to turn back. Even those born in the heavens do not [escape].
One cannot escape the sorrow of being deluded, wild, ignorant, and dull-witted. As for those who enter hell, who can evade the horrors of being flayed, butchered, boiled, and roasted?
Among humans, one is mediocre and things do not go according to one's heart; among animals, they are muddled and devour one another in succession.
For ghosts, there are inexhaustible realms of suffering; for demons, they flaunt their fierce and intoxicated tyranny. Life ends in an instant, and one’s lot is destined for the hells (*niraya*).

In a sudden flash, one revolves through the cycles; there is no staying still. Behold these realms: not a single one is not a retribution for turning away from awakening and uniting with the sensory dust.
When the fundamental nature is ever-awakened, the ocean is vast and the sky is open. When Prajñā lacks its sovereign power, the nets are densely spread. Alas, what a great peril!
That you would wish to tread upon it is like a blind man walking alone through a thicket of thorns at night.

The rain made it pitch black; there was no way to ask for directions. In the end, they lost their bodies and lives, falling into ditches and pits. Their clothes were torn and their bodies wounded, and they did not know where they were.
The suffering in hell is extreme, the mind is clouded, and evil has not yet been extinguished; enduring such pain for long years is truly difficult to bear.
Through a thousand births and ten thousand deaths, the physical form changes; In an instant, the *āpāṇa* demons again test their blades.

(Animals) Piteous indeed, birth and death never cease; Life is cheap, the body light, and the senses dull, yet they still strive for dominance, Committing mutual lust and slaughter. The minds of animals are far too fragmented.
(Ghosts and Spirits) Pale and desolate, drifting and wavering, the sorrowful realm of ghosts; Bitterly and painfully they scurry about, enslaved by wind and thunder.
In their poverty, they further receive the retribution of having their bodies burned; Layer upon layer of illusory shadows, their pain never ceases.
(Human Realm) Having fortunately obtained this human body, one is not yet at peace; A hundred years are but a moment before falling through the barrier of death.
A single grain of counterfeit silver cannot suffice; what can one endure of a lifetime of toil?
(Asura) When the self and others contend for victory and defeat, flying sand and rolling stones strike at the human heart.
The Asuras are intoxicated by the bitterness of war; their souls flee in haste through forests of swords and arrows.
(Heavenly Way) Those who diligently cultivate the ten wholesome deeds may dream of entering heaven; those who seek secret formulas with precision become a host of immortals.
Yet, as long as karmic bonds are not yet extinguished, they remain subject to birth and death; their immeasurable spirits all fall back into the periphery.
Thus, within these six realms and seven destinies, all is dark and obscure, with not a single thing upon which to rely—is this not truly tragic?

There is a path leading home, and your compassionate mother awaits you with the utmost longing. That sentient beings are unfilial is to betray her grace; yet they strive ever more to display their own abilities, straying further from the source.
Holding a single Amitābha Buddha at the back of their minds, how could a thousand spirits or ten thousand saints be able to save them?
Alas! You who slander Prajñā, Chaos your true mind at every turn; Leading you astray through a thousand lifetimes, When will you receive the auspicious sound?
North, south, east, and west; high and low, pure and defiled; throughout the lands of the ten directions, there are infinite sentient beings.

These are the distinctions within the nature of sentient beings, yet they manifest the sameness within Buddha-nature. This is the sameness of the Buddha-mind-nature, which manifests the differences among sentient beings.
To cast aside the boundless ocean and cling instead to this single bubble—how truly pitiable!
It is judged that the two lands are truly separated; the pure and the defiled follow divergent paths with distinct retributions.
Since the matters of the expedient means for rebirth are not taught, who could receive the nectar from the crown of their heads?
In that land, Amitābha Buddha’s lifespan and eon are vast and long; in this land, Śākyamuni World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa early.
Sentient beings have meager merit; they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses. For this reason, Śākyamuni will not remain in the world for long.

Since this defiled land is suffering and human life is brief, he thus brings sentient beings to maturity. Since the Pure Land is blissful and lifespan is immeasurable, he thus gathers in sentient beings.

(The emanation body of Śākyamuni was born here in this Sahā world, within one of the four continents, in Jambudvīpa, in the land of Kapilavastu among the five regions of India. The year of his birth...)

In this land of Zhendan (China), from the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty—the Jia-yin year—until the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu—the Ren-shen year—the Buddha entered nirvana between the twin śāla trees outside the city of Kuśinagara.

Then, in the eleventh year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the Emperor dreamed of a golden man with a halo around his neck flying through the palace halls. He dispatched envoys to seek him in the Western Regions, whereupon they obtained Buddhist scriptures, images, and two Indian monks, who arrived in the eastern lands.

They were enshrined at the Honglu Temple, which was later renamed Baima Temple. Gradually, the various scriptures spread eastward; the three studies flourished in succession, and the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land was also inaugurated.

Those who turn their backs on awakening possess no knowledge; may the Awakened One come to deliver them. Through the power of manifested skillful means, he utterly destroys greed, anger, and delusion.
Formerly, the Great Master Huiyuan was able to rely upon the Buddha’s sincere words to open the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, teaching the people of this region to seek it.
Born in that land, they practice with diligence throughout the six periods of the day and night; the three poisons are extinguished, and they personally behold Amitābha leading them across.
Having shattered the forest of all darkness, he manifests this path of radiant light, whereby those who were enmeshed in the dust of the world depart from it forever.

I hope you will go to the West; when illness arises, the medicine arrives; when hunger strikes, the meal is ready. To use the dust to obscure awakening is to make awakening entirely the dust; yet with awakening—

Breaking through the sensory objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). The entirety of these objects is awakening. The wise person enters into this realization instantaneously; knowing that turning one's back on awakening is erroneous, they remain amidst the objects yet remain detached from them.

Chapter Three: On the Cycle of Saṃsāra If one’s heart desires to seek what is good, one must first inquire within one's own house. This cycle of birth and death is nothing more than a single dream.
If you do not awaken, you will remain in a state of profound slumber; dreaming within a dream, when will it ever come to an end? If you grow weary of this saṃsāra...
Return! The moment a single thought becomes empty, saṃsāra is already shattered. Nevertheless, while it is very easy to speak of this, its realization is difficult.
This is because saṃsāra has a root of its own; as long as that root is not uprooted, there is no place to apply effort.

Entering enlightenment from delusion—this single thought-moment is the true barrier. Only when the struggle between tiger and dragon ceases does one know that transformation is at ease.
Dissipate these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Quiesce these false thoughts (*vikalpa*). What are habitual tendencies? They are that which arise spontaneously when encountering circumstances.

Cease this. It cannot be resolved through the conceptual characteristics of dharmas; everywhere there is only restless coming and going. Therefore, you should dissolve it and let it subside.

The autumn wind blows and leaves fall in profound desolation; can the mind of wild intoxication be paused for a moment?

How many matters of gain and loss are there in this world? When pressed to the limit, the ability to fly is the most excellent strategy.

within these barriers, further barriers arise, and one cannot leap out of this circle. With one great leap, one has already emerged. Yet he has started another circle.

Chapter Four: On the Causes and Conditions of the Pure Land.
How does one find the path? The path lies within the mind. To escape suffering and attain rebirth is not without skillful means;

it is simply that the luminosity of one's own nature is inherently capable of illuminating all phenomena. The infinite environments and beings are clearly manifest; this is precisely for the sake of the body and mind. Based upon—
Regarding the world: the world of body and mind is, in its entirety, a single light. Within this light, one recollects the Buddha and attains rebirth;
this is called the unsurpassed skillful means.
At every place, the banners stand firm as the wind enters meditative concentration; Layer upon layer, the pavilions and towers hold within them a radiant light.
When human hearts reach this place, they are entirely free from defilement; It is all the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s liberation.
The water of eight virtues reflects golden sands; Within the ponds of the seven treasures bloom flowers of the nine grades.
Birds exhort people to diligently recite the Buddha’s name; throughout the six periods of the day, celestial music resounds without clamor.
Amitābha Buddha has Avalokiteśvara on his left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta on his right. The ground is made of gold and adorned with a hundred jewels.
There are no women; there are no Māras or non-Buddhists; there are no beings in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; and there are no asuras.

The golden body of our Buddha shines eternally, Manifesting within the light throughout the worlds of the ten directions;

This is the method for transgressing the three realms horizontally: directly proceeding from this eastern land to the Western Paradise, instantly merging the three grades of practitioners to return to the Land of Peace and Bliss, where lotus flowers naturally emit fragrance upon their unfolding.

Though one may have committed grave sins leading to death, if one practices with utmost sincerity, their merit will immediately prevail. This is what all Buddhas have taught: it is true and not false.

O virtuous ones, while there are buddha-lands in each of the ten directions, why is it that you are specifically exhorted to go to the West?
It is because the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is a desirable place where sentient beings wish to be reborn, and Amitābha Buddha is the one whom sentient beings yearn for.
Beholding them as compassionate parents, one is born into that land; wisdom becomes perfected and spiritual powers are manifested.
Dividing one’s body to save the world, one wanders together with the Buddhas, leading all sentient beings to the other shore of Bodhi, where there is immeasurable bliss.

The true light of the original nature is the essence of the Buddha who is mindfulness. Diligent rebirth is the function of the Buddha who is mindfulness.

Subsuming function into essence, the Buddha-mind is profoundly still. The practitioner must attain both essence and function; only then will they not be in vain, naturally harmonizing with the Way.
The spirit transcends beyond the three realms, while the mind manifests within a single sound; essence and function are clearly present.

There is no need for further elaboration on the heroic power of boundless mindfulness; in short, mindfulness of the Buddha is the true cause and condition for rebirth in the Pure Land, and rebirth therein is the true state of liberation from suffering.

Once one’s feet are planted here, it is difficult to rely upon; many lose their footing.

The bliss of the Pure Land of Amitābha.

To receive the bliss of the Western Land, the various sūtras teach that the single practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is an essential dharma-gate. Furthermore, its benefits are exceedingly great, numbering approximately ten.
This brings great benefit both before and after death. First,
day and night they will constantly be protected by the powerful divine generals of the heavens and their retinues, who remain hidden from sight.

Poisonous dragons cannot harm them at all.

Fifth, they shall not suffer from any calamities of fire or water, nor from enemies, bandits, swords, or arrows; nor shall they undergo imprisonment, shackles, or any form of untimely or unjust death.

Seventh, one’s dreams at night will be upright and clear, or one may dream of the sublime and wondrous physical body of Amitābha Buddha.

I exhort the assembly: do not let this opportunity slip away any longer. I shall now proclaim the verses of Master Lianchi; listen with a single mind.
With single-mindedness and without distraction, according to one's capacity—whether great or small—one attains rebirth in the nine grades;

If a person’s child is rebellious, One may avoid the arising of affectionate attachment; this is precisely the time to practice nianfo.
If a person is without illness, Taking advantage of the body’s robust health; this is precisely the time to practice nianfo.

If a person is old, their remaining days are few; this is precisely the time to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
If a person is young, their spirit is clear and sharp; this is precisely the time to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Chapter Five: On Unfailing Diligence.

"O Great Assembly! Since you already know that the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is most peaceful while this Sahā world is extremely suffering, you should naturally seek to escape this burning house as early as possible.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, this Sahā world is like a burning house and cannot be inhabited for long.
The young children are playing and do not know how to avoid the danger. The elder, possessing wisdom, then uses goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts to lead them out."
"Come out! Come out now quickly! I shall give you these three kinds of carriages. Once the sons had come out, they asked their father for the carriages.
The elder then had great white ox-carts fashioned with immeasurable adornments, so that these sons might enjoy them equally.

The three carriages represent the superior, middling, and inferior faculties; the great white ox-cart represents the entry into the Buddha’s Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), wherein there is nothing equal to it.
They differ. Those of inferior capacity save themselves alone; they are of the class of Arhats. Those of middling capacity save half of others and half of themselves;

if they appear in an age without a Buddha, they are called Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers), but if they appear in an age with a Buddha, they are called Pratyayabuddhas (Dependent Awakeners). Those of superior capacity take the full measure of saving all sentient beings;
they are of the class of Bodhisattvas. When these are brought together, they converge into one, entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, where there are no longer three grades.
The distinction is as follows: for example, Amitābha Buddha manifests the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which is solely the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*) and possesses no two lands.
Nevertheless, to open this one land into three is likewise an application of skillful means; furthermore, one does not cling to the identity of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Just as in the Pure Land of Amitābha, within a single kind of lotus flower, there appear the nine grades of rebirth. The One Vehicle of the Land of Quiescent Light is not separate from the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).
The rebirth through the three vehicles does not depart from the One Vehicle; because it does not depart from the One Vehicle, it employs exclusively the single method of nianfo (buddha-recollection).
Because it does not depart from the three vehicles, the Buddha manifests nine grades of lotus flowers. Nine is three, and three is one;
entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, there is nothing else. Therefore, those who practice nianfo must be diligent in seeking the realm of the Buddha, which is eternally empty.
As for that mind, do not allow it to become attached. When a thought arises, it is immediately the Buddha; let no other matter remain. Respond to conditions and that is all.

This is the name of the One Buddha. Do not dwell on reaching the goal; never cease your effort. Thus, the four characters of "One Mind" (一心) and the "One Mind" of the four characters—when analyzed, they do not separate;
when joined, they leave no trace. It is not a joining, for fundamentally there are not two. Nor is it one, nor is it...
It is not that they are not one. To recollect the Buddha in this way, with such single-mindedness, is true diligence.
When the task of diligence is accomplished, never allow the mind to become coarse. With single-mindedness and without regression, the flower blooms and the precious moon descends.

To apply the mind during the seven days is to practice with courageous diligence. To apply the mind in dedicating merit and making vows during the morning and evening services is to practice with constant diligence.
If one realizes the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka* through sudden awakening, it is both sudden and perfect;
neither born nor a Buddha, the ten realms are unified as one, and the three bodies are merged into emptiness. A single phrase of Amitābha—furthermore...
There is no other matter; when the dimensions of the mind, whether horizontal or vertical, are shattered until nothing remains, that is most supreme.
An ancient said: "The boundless ocean of lands contains the void within its waves; From the ocean and the void, the Lotus Palace appears.
The Lotus Palace pervades everywhere throughout the ocean of the void; Within this ocean of the void, Amitābha’s countenance alone is revealed."
This Dharma-realm is unimpeded and perfectly interfused; it is indeed boundless vigor. That which is boundless vigor is precisely this Buddha of the present single thought-moment.
This thought of a single Buddha is neither universal nor particular, neither identical nor different, neither formed nor destroyed;
yet it is both universal and particular, both identical and different, and both formed and destroyed.

The diagram states: "If one raises any single dharma, all six dharmas are fully present; they are unimpeded and perfectly interfused. This can be seen by reflecting upon it. (Regarding these six characteristics, there are analogies provided in the *Zongjing lu*;

here, I shall now attempt to imitate that explanation. For example, a person’s entire body is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). The head, torso, hands, and feet are the particular characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The fact that the head, torso, hands, and feet are all the body is the characteristic of sameness (*samatā-lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the head is not the torso.)

The feet are not the hands; this is the aspect of difference (*visama-lakṣaṇa*). When the head, eyes, hands, and feet gather together to form a single body, this is the aspect of formation (*siddhi-lakṣaṇa*). When the head is high and the abdomen is broad, and the hands and feet each occupy their respective left and right positions, dispersing to abide in their own places, this is the aspect of disintegration (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*).

Disintegration means separation; formation means conjunction. Difference means non-identity; sameness means identity. Particularity means partiality; totality means wholeness. If one takes the head, eyes, hands, and feet of a single body as the subject of discourse, then totality and particularity, sameness and difference, formation and disintegration are all manifested simultaneously.
All phenomena are likewise so. Furthermore, this very Buddha of the present moment—this one Buddha—[is thus].
Mindfulness is itself the true thread; in the true thread, there is no place to be sought. Its diagram says: Sea:
(A single drop of water contains the flavor of a hundred rivers.
Mirror: (A mirror one foot square reflects images from a thousand li away.)
Gold (Though sentient beings may be wicked, the Buddha-nature within their hearts remains unchanging; it is like pure gold that, though burned or buried, retains its original yellow color).
Lamp (A thousand lamps in a single room: their light is neither identical nor different).
Moon (The moon on the eighth day: its orb carries both darkness and brightness).
Vase: (Within a crystal vase, mustard seeds appear one by one, all manifest at once.

Take up one thread, and all ten threads are present; they are unimpeded and perfectly interfused. This can be seen by reflecting upon it. (These ten threads are found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.)

In the *Shu-chao* (Commentary), there are ten names; these are also further indicated in the *Wu-jiao-yi* (Ritual of the Five Teachings) and the *Chang-er-lun* (Treatise on the Elder). I shall now record them following the ten characters. First, the character "Sea" (*hai*) refers to the Gate of Simultaneous Fulfillment and Correspondence. Second, the character "Mirror" (*jing*).

The ninth character, "Dream" (夢), is the gate of the unimpeded mastery of breadth and narrowness. The third character, "Gold" (金), is the gate of the sovereign identity of all phenomena. The fourth character, "Lamp" (燈), is the gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without confusion. The fifth character, "Moon" (月), is the gate of the secret, simultaneous fusion of the hidden and the manifest.

The sixth character, "Vase" (瓶), is the gate of the subtle containment and establishment of phenomena. The seventh character, "Jewel" (珠), is the gate of the interpenetration of light and shadow. The eighth character, "Fist" (拳), is the gate of manifesting the Dharma by relying on mundane events to generate understanding. The ninth character, "Dream" (夢) [is as follows].

This is the gate of the distinct formation of phenomena separated by ten ages. The tenth character, *xing* (star), is the gate of the perfect fusion and complete virtue of the principal and its attendants. There is no boundless diligence that possesses a discriminating mind regarding east and west or purity and defilement;
yet there is no absence of the manifest events of Buddhas appearing and departing. Thus it is for every phenomenon, and thus it is for every mind.
Viewing the two lands as mere motes of dust, one relies upon the single True Suchness as a dream from yesterday. Those of the highest-grade spiritual capacity are able to save.
The lowest of the low does not stagnate in the middling of the middling; originally, there are neither upper nor lower grades. This is boundless diligence, which I have previously praised.
One Buddha, Amitābha, completely pervades the Dharma-realm; the reflections of lapis lazuli appear throughout empty space.
The eastern land and the western soil are fundamentally without obstruction; the lotus flowers that blossom are ten times more red.
I also praise this constant diligence. Abiding in truth, the mind is ever sublime;
All dharmas are efficacious through their application, for the Buddha possesses divine power.
Do not let your time pass in vain; within the Lotus Land, you shall turn the wheel of Dharma.
I always praise this courageous diligence.
Its great essence is perfectly integrated, transcending day and night; with single-minded resolve one proceeds directly toward the light.
As the sound of the voice reaches the lotus, it causes the flower to bloom; how could there be further wandering in saṃsāra or the arising of inequality?
Diligence enters through sound. Among the six sense faculties, the ear is the most vacuous and sensitive; the tongue faculty issues forth, while the ear faculty receives within.

[Yet] the phlegmatic, the subtle, and the elegant tones create waves beneath the tongue;
lacking maturity, they are no different from a buffoon, easily moved by the ears of fickle children. Where is their majestic light? [End of Section]
The brush exhausts itself, yet lewd sounds remain unexpunged; describing such gallantry is the greatest malady of the talented man. I urge you:
abandon the causes and conditions of flowery speech, and maintain total purity day and night.
For the sake of this trivial physical body, one exerts oneself to vie with gold and silver for the sake of wife and children.

Exhausting every inch and foot, what was first full now vies for every measure; the ravines and gullies are difficult to fill (greed arises because of what is desirable). Why is this? Because the mind has not yet been satisfied. I urge you:
if the causes and conditions of greed are entirely restrained by purity (if the mind is inexhaustible, then desire will likewise be inexhaustible).
Anger fills the breast; the Dragon Spring sword in its scabbard seems about to cry out. With a single thought of heavenly harmony, the six realms of the asuras are diminished.
Afflictions have no city; do not lose yourself in the nature of mind. When self and others are both forgotten, all things are as cold as ashes.
I exhort you: guard against the causes and conditions of the karma of anger; let all be pure.

A single flavor of ignorance makes one an ordinary person (the three delusions all arise from ignorance). Once you understand the capacity of your own faculties, do not despise its dullness (cause and effect are subtle and wondrous).

First, you must have faith in cause and effect (who is it that possesses true faith?). Wisdom belongs to the nature; what is there to cultivate or realize? The mirror of the mind hangs solitary, storing not even a hair’s breadth of reflection. I exhort you:
regarding the causes and conditions of deluded karma, refrain from them all and maintain purity.
